nameStory: The "yellow soot" name comes from this lichen's distinctive yellowish spore-bearing structures that can look like tiny dots of colored soot dusting old wood. The scientific name Calicium means "little cup," referring to the cup-like fruiting bodies that release clouds of yellow spores when mature.
description: Yellow soot lichen is a crusty, wood-dwelling lichen that forms thin, grayish patches on weathered wood surfaces. It's most noticeable for its tiny yellow-brown stalked fruiting bodies that stick up like miniature pins from the lichen's surface. The whole organism typically covers just a few inches of wood surface, creating subtle patches that are easy to overlook unless you're looking closely. This is one of the "pin lichens" - a group known for their distinctive upright spore-producing structures.

idTips.label: Stalked fruiting bodies
idTips.description: Look for tiny pin-like structures about 1mm tall with yellowish-brown heads that stick up from the lichen surface - these release powdery yellow spores when disturbed

idTips.label: Wood substrate
idTips.description: Always found growing on weathered wood, especially old fence posts, barn siding, or fallen logs - never on bark of living trees

idTips.label: Crusty texture
idTips.description: The main lichen body feels rough and crusty to the touch, forming thin grayish to whitish patches that seem almost painted onto the wood surface

idTips.label: Yellow spore dust
idTips.description: Gently tap mature specimens and watch for tiny puffs of yellow powder - this distinctive spore release is visible on calm days

idTips.label: Weathered wood preference
idTips.description: Most abundant on sun-exposed, gray weathered wood that feels dry and rough - rarely found on fresh-cut or painted surfaces

habitat: Yellow soot lichen thrives on old wooden structures throughout New England, especially weathered fence posts, barn siding, and abandoned buildings in rural areas. It prefers sunny, dry locations where the wood has turned gray from years of weather exposure. You'll also find it on old fallen logs in open woodlands, but it's much more common on human-made wooden structures than in deep forest settings.

seasonality.spring: Fruiting bodies begin developing as temperatures warm, appearing as tiny bumps on the lichen surface. This is when spore production starts to ramp up.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for spore release - the yellow fruiting heads are most prominent and active during warm, dry weather. Light tapping will produce visible spore clouds.
seasonality.fall: Fruiting bodies remain visible and may continue releasing spores during dry periods. The lichen prepares for winter dormancy as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: The crusty lichen body persists through cold weather, though fruiting bodies may be less prominent. Best time to notice the overall growth pattern without distracting spore activity.

funFact: This tiny lichen can turn a simple fence post into a biological spore cannon - on dry summer days, even a gentle breeze or the vibration from a passing truck can trigger dozens of these microscopic "pins" to simultaneously puff out clouds of yellow spores that can travel for miles to colonize new wooden surfaces.
confusionNotes: Other pin lichens in the stubble lichen group look very similar, but yellow soot lichen is the most common species on old fence posts and weathered lumber. If you find pin lichens on tree bark instead of dead wood, you're likely looking at a different species entirely. Remember: wood-dwelling with yellow spores = yellow soot lichen.
contextualKnowledge: Note that some field guides may list this species under the genus Cyphelium rather than Calicium - both names refer to the same organism, but taxonomists have moved it between these closely related genera over the years. Don't be confused if you see both scientific names in different sources.
compareHints: Yellow soot lichen differs from its Calicium relatives primarily by its strong preference for dead wood rather than tree bark, and its consistently yellow spore production. Yellow collar stubble lichen grows on bark and has more orange tones, while other Calicium species tend to have darker or more brownish fruiting bodies. The wood-dwelling habitat is your best clue for distinguishing this species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Yellow collar stubble lichen differs from its cousin yellow soot lichen by having that distinctive yellow pruina collar and growing primarily on wood rather than various surfaces.
Fir pin differs from its stubble lichen relatives primarily in its strong preference for coniferous trees and its particularly prominent black pins.
Compared to its relatives like Yellow Collar Stubble Lichen, this species lacks the distinctive yellow coloring around the stalk bases.
